author: Front Row Feels
title: Stay Awake and Watch the Flowers Grow
text:
I’d been listening to Jacob Alon for a while before TRNSMT but had never had the pleasure of seeing them live. I already knew every word to Don’t Fall Asleep and naturally looked forward to singing along to a song I’d come to feel incredibly connected to.
Instead, I found myself standing at the barrier completely speechless.
With nowhere else to look and nothing else competing for my attention, I realised I wasn't singing anymore. I was too busy watching. Watching someone with extraordinary talent perform a song I'd loved for months in a way that somehow made me hear it completely differently.
It takes a special kind of artist to shut this gal up. Jacob Alon managed it without even trying. Weeks later, it’s still one of the moments from TRNSMT that I find myself coming back to the most. So, I thought it deserved something a little more than a paragraph buried in a festival roundup. Whether you're already familiar with Jacob's music or you're meeting them here for the first time, grab a brew and let's chat.
I’ve always thought grief must be one of the hardest things to write about because no two people carry it in quite the same way. We all bring our own people, our own memories and our own unanswered questions to songs like this. Don’t Fall Asleep has always made me cry, but probably not for the reasons it does somebody else.
It reminds me of somebody I admired deeply who died far too young in tragic circumstances. It was the first time I’d really experienced grief. He loved music, and one of my favourite memories of him is him playing guitar while I sang. Truthfully, every time I hear Matthew tracing the life he would’ve known, I think about him. I’m older now than he ever got to be. Somehow the song makes me wonder whether, wherever he is, he got to see the life he never had. I find that thought both heartbreaking and strangely comforting.
Jacob has spoken about writing Don't Fall Asleep from the imagined perspective of a cousin they never met, who died before they were born. Rather than dwelling on the tragedy itself, they imagine Matthew tracing the life he never got to have. It's an astonishing piece of songwriting because it doesn't tell us how to grieve. Instead it creates enough space for us to bring our own grief to it.
The more I've read and listened to Jacob speak, the more it all makes sense. They often talk about songwriting as a way of connecting with other people. There never seems to be any pressure to explain difficult emotions or resolve them. Instead, they write songs that leave room for listeners to bring their own experiences, their own memories and, in my case, a sense of grief that has stayed with me for the last decade.
Whether they're writing about identity, faith, belonging or grief, there's a noticeable absence of judgement. Jacob never seems interested in telling us what to think or how to feel. They simply trust that if they're honest enough, somebody else will find themselves in the song.
Nowhere is that clearer than on Confession. Jacob describes the song as “a shedding of shame” and, having heard it live, I can’t think of a more fitting description. Written after an encounter with someone who would rather deny their shared history than acknowledge it, the song explores what happens when love is pushed into silence by shame. More specifically, it examines the shame so often imposed on queer people; the feeling that something as ordinary and beautiful as love should be hidden away.
That context makes “Was I the one that muddied your mind?” all the more devastating. It’s the sort of question so many of us ask ourselves when we’re trying to make sense of rejection. We start turning everything over, wondering whether we somehow caused another person’s inability to love us openly. The lyric never answers the question, because there often isn’t one. It simply captures the spiral of self-doubt with painful accuracy.
Perhaps that’s why something that happened more recently got under my skin quite as much as it did. Jacob has been supporting Lewis Capaldi on his current run of shows and, alongside plenty of people discovering and loving their music, came a pretty grim wave of comments online. We all know my feelings on the way people speak about artists on the internet these days, and I will probably never stop talking about it. It also rarely escapes me that so much of this nastiness seems to be reserved for people who don’t fit neatly into what others expect an artist to look like or be.
I’m very much aware that nobody has to enjoy every support act they see. What bothered me was how quickly some of the conversation moved away from the music entirely. Jacob was there to perform their music to an audience who perhaps hadn’t encountered them before, yet plenty of the comments had very little to say about the actual art. Instead, people picked apart Jacob’s appearance and the way they presented themselves, enough that Jacob eventually addressed the abuse themselves.
Their response was brilliant. Speaking on stage between songs, Jacob acknowledged the abuse they’d been receiving and the fact that, in their own words, they “look a bit different.” Rather than allowing that to make them retreat, they did the exact opposite.
“I’ve been getting a lot of abuse actually, online, from the last shows. I look a bit different. So I’m going to double down. This is a song for the gays, and the trans people, and everyone in between. And if you don’t like that, you can fuck off and rant about it on Facebook, ya cunts.”
Here is an artist being made to feel that the way they present themselves is something other people are entitled to pick apart, and their answer is to take up even more space as exactly that person.
I think we have a strange relationship with authenticity in music. We say we want artists to be completely themselves, but there still seems to be an unspoken limit on what that is allowed to look like. The second somebody falls outside of what feels familiar, their difference becomes something to comment on. That feels particularly backwards when the very thing that makes Jacob’s work so special is how much of themselves they are willing to put into it.
Perhaps the loveliest consequence of that openness is what has happened since In Limerence made its way into other people’s lives. Jacob has spoken about hearing from listeners who have found meanings in the record that they had never consciously considered while writing it.
There’s something incredible about that. You can write something from the most specific and personal place imaginable, send it out into the world and somehow it ends up helping a complete stranger make sense of something entirely different. I’ve spent a large chunk of this essay proving that without meaning to. Don’t Fall Asleep was written with Matthew in mind, yet became tangled up with somebody from my own life who Jacob could never possibly have known existed.
There is something quite wonderful about the fact that this exchange appears to work both ways. Listeners find pieces of themselves in Jacob’s songs, and hearing what those songs have come to mean to other people seems to have given something back to Jacob too. Maybe that’s one of the greatest things music can do. Something that begins with one person trying to understand themselves can end up making thousands of other people feel a little more understood too.
I learned while reading about Jacob for this piece that they dropped out of university to pursue music full-time and, my goodness, I am glad they did.
There is obviously an extraordinary amount of talent there. The voice alone is enough to stop you in your tracks, but the more time I spend with Jacob’s work, the more impressed I am by the thought and care that sits behind it. These are songs that deserve to be properly listened to. Seeing them performed live only made me appreciate that more. I look forward to the next time I am able to do this.
I think what has really endeared me to Jacob goes beyond the music. Everything I’ve watched and read from them suggests somebody who cares deeply about the people their songs reach. The way they speak about listeners finding their own meanings in In Limerence, the love they have for the queer community who find something of themselves in Confession, even the decision to meet a wave of nastiness with a C-bomb — there is something incredibly lovely about an artist who seems determined to make other people feel a little more comfortable being themselves too.
I walked away from that TRNSMT set with an enormous amount of admiration for the person behind the music. The world could do with more Jacob Alons. Artists willing to make strange, beautiful, deeply personal work and trust that somebody out there will understand it. People willing to double down on who they are when the world suggests they should do the opposite.
And selfishly, I’m just very glad one of them decided to drop out of uni.
